## Paper

- Title: **Accelerator Choice Is Not Enough: AlphaFold2 Inference on Cloud TPUs**
- Authors: **Lorenzo Pazienza** (LUISS Guido Carli University, Rome, Italy) and **Ihab El Bani** (Al Akhawayn University, Ifrane, Morocco)
- arXiv ID: **arXiv:2609.34818** · primary category cs.DC, cross-listed cs.LG and cs.PF
- DOI: **10.48550/arXiv.2609.34818** (https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2609.34818)
- Abstract page: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34818
- PDF: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.34818
- LaTeX source in repo: https://github.com/lorenzopazienza/alphafold-tpu-benchmark/tree/main/paper/preprint/source
- Submitted 28 September 2026. The paper cites commit a63e955 of the repository (tag arxiv-v1), and every number in it traces to `paper/data/canonical_results.md`.

**Central message:** this is not a “TPUs are hundreds of times faster” result. The hardware gap is real but campaign-specific; the finding is that the software layer, how the work is expressed in JAX, decides how much of an eight-chip TPU slice a user actually gets.

**BibTeX:**
```
@misc{pazienza2026accelerator,
  title         = {Accelerator Choice Is Not Enough: {AlphaFold2} Inference on Cloud {TPUs}},
  author        = {Pazienza, Lorenzo and El Bani, Ihab},
  year          = {2026},
  eprint        = {2609.34818},
  archivePrefix = {arXiv},
  primaryClass  = {cs.DC},

  url           = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34818}
}
```

## Section 1 - Hero (`#top`)

**On-screen layout:** Two-column hero. Left: kicker + title + blurb + links. Right: giant “1 / 8” metric over a stacked list of software choices.

- Kicker: arXiv:2609.34818 · cs.DC · September 2026
- Title: Accelerator Choice Is Not Enough
- Subtitle: AlphaFold2 Inference on Cloud TPUs
- Body: “AlphaFold2 runs the same JAX code on CPUs, GPUs and Google Cloud TPUs, so the accelerator looks like the main decision a user has to make. We show that it is not. On an eight-chip TPU v5e slice, the default execution path uses one chip, and how the work is expressed in JAX decides how much of the hardware a user actually gets.”
- Links: Paper (arXiv) · PDF · Code · Cite
- Metric label: TPU v5e-8, default execution path
- Metric: **1 / 8** (teal “/ 8”), captioned “chips hold data”
- Stacked list under the metric, one row per software choice:
  1. Default path (jax.jit) - 1 of 8 chips used (gray dot)
  2. Batching with jax.vmap - never above single-query throughput (blue dot)
  3. Mapping with jax.pmap - 6.53-7.91× the throughput of one chip (teal dot)
  4. Automatic sharding - per-chip footprint unchanged (463 MB) (gray dot)
- Context label under the list: single chip, steady state 0.47 s per call against 13.1 s on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 (August 2026 campaign)
- Footer credit line under a hairline rule: Lorenzo Pazienza (LUISS Guido Carli University) & Ihab El Bani (Al Akhawayn University) · Work carried out in Stanford’s ME344, High Performance Computing and AI Systems, Summer Session 2026

## Section 2 - Paper (`#paper`)

- Kicker: Paper
- Headline: “Accelerator Choice Is Not Enough: AlphaFold2 Inference on Cloud TPUs”
- Byline on page: Lorenzo Pazienza, Ihab El Bani · arXiv preprint, September 2026 · cs.DC
- Left column: the abstract, collapsed to three lines with a “Read the abstract” toggle
- Links row: arXiv page · PDF · LaTeX source · Code and data
- Right column: a dark, horizontally scrollable BibTeX block with a Copy button (see the BibTeX above), then the note “The paper cites commit a63e955 of the repository (tag arxiv-v1). Every number in it traces to paper/data/canonical_results.md.”

**Abstract (verbatim):** AlphaFold2 is written in JAX, so the same inference code compiles and runs unchanged on CPUs, GPUs and Google Cloud TPUs. That portability makes the accelerator look like the main decision a user has to make. We show that it is not. Running one AlphaFold2 inference workload across a Colab CPU runtime, an NVIDIA T4 GPU and a dedicated eight-chip Cloud TPU v5e slice, we find a large hardware advantage for the TPU, 0.47 s per call in steady state on a single chip against 13.1 s on the T4 in the same measurement campaign, and three ways in which the software layer decides how much of it a user actually gets. The default execution path uses one chip of the eight, and at list prices the idle capacity makes the slice cost about as much per prediction as the GPU. Batching with JAX’s vmap never exceeds single-query throughput, while mapping queries across chips with JAX’s pmap gives eight chips 6.5-7.9x the throughput of one on a matched grid; automatic sharding leaves the per-chip footprint unchanged, consistent with replication, most plausibly because AlphaFold2 carries no sharding annotations. Our retained trace analysis of a first call at a new input shape reports about three quarters of the traced span in JAX tracing and compilation rather than execution. Reruns five weeks later reproduced neither cloud baseline, the GPU one off by roughly a factor of two, so the hardware ratio above is specific to one campaign.

---

## Section 3 - Problem (`#problem`)

- Kicker: Question
- Headline: “What decides the performance a user actually gets?”
- Body: The problem - biology needs a protein’s 3D shape; AlphaFold 2 (DeepMind) made high-accuracy structure prediction practical with a large JAX/Haiku Evoformer, but running that inference is expensive and opaque across accelerators: cold XLA compiles, underused TPU pods, unclear CPU vs GPU vs TPU trade-offs. What we did - ran AlphaFold2’s JAX forward pass on a Google Colab CPU runtime (Intel Xeon, 2 vCPU), a Google Colab NVIDIA Tesla T4 and a Stanford GKE TPU v5e-8 slice (`tpu-v5-lite-podslice`, 2×4, 8 chips). Single-query timings use the same 118-residue input, `model_3`, 0 recycles and randomly initialized parameters on every backend. Then we asked where the time goes on a first call, and what it takes to put all eight chips to work.
- Follow-up note: AlphaFold 3 (a separate diffusion codebase) on the same Google Colab Intel Xeon CPU and NVIDIA Tesla T4, plus a confirmed finding that its public release does not support TPU.

---

## Section 4 - Approach (`#approach`)

- Kicker: System topology
- Headline: “One script, three backends”
- Body: Docker for the CPU/GPU images; Kubernetes Job + Kueue on GKE for the TPU worker (`tpu-v5-lite-podslice`). The single-query baseline calls `spike_tpu_forward_pass.py` with AlphaFold2 `model_3`, 0 recycles and a 118-residue input on every backend. The multi-chip and scaling-grid experiments use a different synthetic input family, so their numbers are compared among themselves, not with the single-query baseline.

**Architecture strip (4 cells):**
1. Script - `spike_tpu_forward_pass.py` (AF2 `model_3`, 0 recycles, 118 residues)
2. CPU - Google Colab Intel Xeon · 2 vCPU → `result_cpu-colab.json`
3. GPU - Google Colab NVIDIA Tesla T4 → `result_gpu-t4.json`
4. TPU - Stanford GKE v5e-8 · 2×4 lite (`tpu-v5-lite-podslice`) → `result_tpu + traces`

**Parameters note:** AF2 systems timings use Haiku random init so the same compiled graph is exercised without downloading trained weights. The ubiquitin structure lower down the page is separate (ESMFold with trained weights, for biology, not for the clocks). AlphaFold 3 uses its own notebooks and Jobs.

---

## Section 5 - Results (`#results`)

- Kicker: Single-chip comparison · August 2026 campaign
- Headline: “Steady-state latency, one chip”
- Big callout: **0.47s**
- Subcopy: model_3, 0 recycles, 118-residue input, Haiku random-init. Backends: Google Colab Intel Xeon (2 vCPU), Google Colab NVIDIA Tesla T4, Stanford GKE TPU v5e-8 (2×4 lite). Identical code path; bar lengths are log-scaled.

**Latency bars (log-scaled widths on page):**
| Backend | Display time | Speedup vs CPU | Bar color (approx) |
|---------|--------------|----------------|--------------------|
| CPU Xeon (Google Colab, 2 vCPU) | 212.1s | 1× (CPU baseline) | gray |
| GPU Tesla T4 (Google Colab) | 13.1s | 16.2× vs CPU | blue |
| TPU v5e-8 (Stanford GKE, 2×4) | 0.47s | 451× vs CPU | teal |

Note under the bars: the TPU figure is one chip of the eight in the slice, and the speedups are relative to the August CPU baseline.

### Did the baselines reproduce?
No. The CPU and GPU headline figures are August 2026 single-call measurements. Five weeks later both backends were rerun from a committed revision of the benchmark script and **neither reproduced**: CPU steady state rose from 212.113s (n=1) to 348.861 ± 4.690s, 351.891 ± 4.303s and 359.273 ± 2.787s across three September sessions (n=5 each), 1.64-1.69× slower; GPU steady state fell from 13.086s (n=1) to 6.567 ± 0.057s (n=5), roughly 2× faster. The two moved in opposite directions and no cause was isolated. The 451× figure (vs CPU) and the ~27.8× TPU-over-GPU figure divide an August CPU or GPU baseline by the TPU steady state, and both numerators moved on rerun; no TPU rerun exists, because the cluster was a course allocation that ended with the course. Treat those ratios as specific to one measurement campaign, not as portable hardware constants. Raw reruns: `results/repro/`.

**First predict / steady-state (compile visibility):**
| Backend | Ratio | Note |
|---------|-------|------|
| CPU Xeon | 1.28× as timed, ~1.11× corrected | Mostly compute; 36.00s of profiler finalisation sat inside the timer |
| GPU Tesla T4 | 7.46× as timed, ~4.25× corrected | Compile is visible; 42.02s of profiler finalisation sat inside the timer |
| TPU v5e-8 | 59.1× as timed | Cold path is compile. Not correctable: no TPU run log survives |

In a retained trace of one TPU first call, about 76% of the traced `apply_fn` span is self time in JAX’s tracing and compilation path rather than device execution.

**Important:** GPU speedup vs CPU is **16.2×**. TPU vs GPU is ~27.8×. Do not say GPU is 27.8× vs CPU.

---

## Section 6 - Experiments (`#experiments`)

- Kicker: Experiments
- Headline: “Twelve TPU follow-ups”
- UX note on page: Click + on a row for method notes. Shared figures sit under each phase. Amber rail = negative result.

### Phase: Scaling

#### 01 Sequence length - **14.6×** (time for 8.3× length)
- Finding: Steady-state time grew faster than sequence length (8.3× length → 14.6× time).
- Notes: Swept 60, 120, 250, 500 residues. Super-linear; matches pair representation. Compile ~flat.

#### 02 Recycle depth - **~0.46s** (per extra recycle)
- Finding: Steady-state rose linearly with recycles; compile did not.
- Notes: 0/1/3 recycles; ~0.46s each added recycle. Compile jumps 0→1 then flat 1→3.

#### 03 Chip visibility - **1 of 8** (chips used)
- Finding: 1 visible chip and 8 visible chips gave the same single-query time.
- Notes: Default path one query on one chip. 2-/4-chip libtpu flag attempts failed.

### Media C - Shared scaling charts
- URL: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/figures/scaling_charts.png
- Caption: “Left: sequence length. Right: recycle depth. Same TPU v5e-8 runs.”
- **What it shows:** Two side-by-side line charts for TPU v5e-8. Left: latency vs sequence length; right: latency vs recycle depth (118 residues). Each panel plots orange “compile + run (1st call)” and blue “steady-state (2nd call)”. Orange sits much higher; blue rises with length/recycles more gently.

### Phase: Bottleneck & fix

#### 04 Profiler trace - **76%** (of the traced apply_fn span in cache_miss)
- Finding: cache_miss in JAX pjit accounted for ~76% of the traced apply_fn span, not of the whole first predict call.
- Notes: `$pjit.py:250` ~12.55s self-time inside a 16.56s traced span; the full first predict is 27.78s, so the two are different captures. TPU device nearly idle → host-side JIT. Reported from profiling/trace_analysis.md; the raw trace is not in the repository.

#### 05 Compilation cache - **6.81×** (faster init_params)
- Finding: Persisting the JAX compile cache across a process restart cut init_params by 6.81× (66.48s → 20.72s).
- Notes: First predict also improved 1.90× with a warm cache; steady-state unchanged.

#### 06 Precision (bf16) - **−40%** (steady-state HBM)
- Finding: bfloat16 cut steady-state HBM ~40% with little runtime change at this size.
- Notes: Wall-clock barely moved; peak memory briefly higher during cast.

### Phase: Multi-chip

#### 07 Multi-query batching - **lower** (proteins/sec vs batch=1) · NEGATIVE
- Finding: jax.vmap never beat batch=1; only TPU_0 used HBM.
- Notes: At batch 1, 2, 4 and 8 measured throughput was 2.051, 1.928, 1.487 and 1.508 proteins/sec, that is 0.94×, 0.73× and 0.74× the batch-1 rate. The decline is not monotonic (batch 8 is marginally above batch 4), so the values are reported as measured rather than fitted. Memory stayed on one chip. vmap stacks work inside a single compiled program; it does not place work on the other seven chips.

### Media D - Batching chart
- URL: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/figures/batching_chart.png
- Caption: “Wall-clock rises with batch size; per-protein cost worsens vs batch=1.”
- **What it shows:** Chart of batching experiment outcomes: wall-clock grows with batch size and per-protein throughput falls to 0.94×, 0.73× and 0.74× of batch=1; reinforces that vmap did not spread work across the 8-chip slice.

#### 08 pmap parallelism - **6.92×** (throughput over the single-query baseline)
- Finding: jax.pmap ran 8 proteins on 8 chips at 6.92× the single-query, single-chip throughput (86.5% parallel efficiency). That baseline uses a different input family, so the like-for-like figure is the matched chip-count grid: 6.53× at 100 residues (81.6% efficiency) rising to 7.91× at 1000 (98.9%).
- Notes: 2.13 → 14.72 proteins/sec; per-chip HBM 644 MB on TPU_0 and 445–469 MB on the other seven, each close to a single-protein footprint, which matches eight independent runs rather than one replicated copy.

#### 09 Auto-sharding (auto-mesh) - **463 MB** (per chip, unchanged) · NEGATIVE
- Finding: auto-mesh left the per-chip footprint unchanged at ~463 MB, the single-chip figure (one recorded scalar per run) - consistent with replication.
- Notes: Best explanation - AlphaFold's Haiku modules carry no sharding annotations for the partitioner to propagate from; a hypothesis, not confirmed from retained compiler evidence. Which partitioner ran is not recorded: the Job pins `jax[tpu]==0.10.2`, which defaults to Shardy, and sets no flag. Reproduced twice.

#### 10 External ensemble across chips - **8/8** (chips with nonzero memory)
- Finding: Built an ensemble outside the model with pmap + cross-device pmean; all 8 chips report nonzero memory and an allclose check on the first and last returned replicas passes.
- Notes: AlphaFold source untouched; 8 members with their own random seeds, one per chip, averaged with a real `jax.lax.pmean` on raw predicted_lddt logits. Steady-state 0.538s. No speedup was measured against a sequential eight-member run, so the experiment carries no throughput or cost claim. Per-chip HBM 427–624 MB (not the flat 463 MB replication signature). Scope: distributed ensembling for one query, not full Evoformer tensor sharding.

### Phase: Fit & rigor

#### 11 Empirical scaling law - **R² 0.981** (16-point TPU grid)
- Finding: Power law on 16 TPU runs (4 chip counts × 4 lengths) fits R² 0.981.
- Equation: throughput ≈ 4527.77 · chips^0.963 · length^−1.572
- Implication: chip exponent near 1 → pmap scaling holds across the lengths tested. The fit is a summary of this grid rather than a model of it: per length it over-predicts by 10-26% at 100 residues and 23-32% at 1000, and under-predicts at 250 and 500. Tested against the measured grid rather than the fit, cost per prediction is nearly flat in chip count only at long sequences: +22.6% from 1 to 8 chips at 100 residues, about +1% at 1000.

### Media E - Scaling law chart
- URL: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/figures/scaling_law_chart.png
- Caption: “Throughput vs chips and sequence length on the measured grid.”
- **What it shows:** Visualization of the 16-run grid / fit: throughput rising with chip count and falling with sequence length, consistent with the fitted power law (R² 0.981). Descriptive fit; deviations from the measured grid reach 32%.

#### 12 Model pick & repeats - **0.12%** (CV on steady state, 3 repeats)
- Finding: model_5's steady state took 0.403 s against 0.471 s for model_3 (14.4% less time); model_4 took 0.472 s, the same as model_3. Three repeats stayed at or below 1% CV.
- Notes: Across three repeats of one configuration the coefficient of variation was 0.12% on steady state, 0.82% on init_params and 1.00% on the first predict, so the model gap is far above the run-to-run noise.

---

## Section 7 - AlphaFold 3 (`#af3`)

- Kicker: Side investigation
- Headline: “AlphaFold 3 on the same backends”
- Body: Separate DeepMind codebase (Pairformer + diffusion - not an AF2 version bump). Same 118-residue toy input, seed=1. Trained weights ~1.15 GB. Five diffusion samples per call.

### AlphaFold 3 model inference (one seed, five diffusion samples, identical Google Colab)
| Backend | AF3 model inference |
|---------|---------------------|
| CPU (Google Colab) | 2401.38s |
| GPU T4 (Google Colab) | 86.21s |

CPU→GPU speedup **27.86×**, compilation included on both sides. No AF3/AF2 ratio is reported: the two models differ in recycling depth, in whether the timed region includes compilation, and in samples per call, so per-prediction ratios between them are not interpretable.

### Media F - Interactive AF3 3D viewer + confidence chart
- Same component pattern as ubiquitin (`ProteinViewer` + 3Dmol.js).
- CIF: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/structure/af3_toy_test_cpu-colab_model.cif
- Fallback still: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/figures/af3_toy_test_structure.png
- On-page kicker: “AlphaFold 3 · structure”
- Title: “AF3 toy structure”
- Subtitle: Diffusion sample, seed 1 · 118 residues, no MSA · **ptm 0.23**
- **What the 3D shows:** Cartoon ribbon colored by per-atom confidence (CIF `B_iso_or_equiv`, same pLDDT color scale as ubiquitin). Expect mostly orange/yellow (low–medium), not blue - correct for this input.
- **What the chart shows:** Per-residue CA confidence for residues 1–118; values roughly ~23–61 (mean CA ~43). No shaded C-term band (unlike ubiquitin).
- Caption (stated on site): “Low confidence throughout - expected for a no-MSA input, not a defect. Not comparable to the ubiquitin mean pLDDT above.”
- **Cross-model quality note:** Do **not** treat AF3 ptm 0.23 / low CA confidence vs ubiquitin mean pLDDT 90.5 as a head-to-head model-quality ranking. The AF3 toy run deliberately has no MSA.

### TPU wall (negative result)
- Every infrastructure step worked (native build, CCD, weights, `jax[tpu]` on Stanford v5e-8 Job).
- Inference died at flag validation: public AF3 `--jax_backend` only accepts `cpu | gpu | mps`.
- Log: `FATAL Flags parsing error: flag --jax_backend=tpu: value should be one of <cpu|gpu|mps>`
- Matches DeepMind docs (NVIDIA GPU ≥7.0 or CPU). Not an infra miss on our side.

---

## Section 8 - Cost (`#cost`)

- Kicker: Cost
- Headline: “Idle chips cost as much as busy ones”
- Body: At list prices, the default path’s seven idle chips make the TPU slice cost about the same per prediction as the T4: $1.25 vs $1.27 per 1,000 predictions (CPU $11.19), on the August baselines. Rented one chip at a time, the same TPU work would cost $0.157 per 1,000, about 8.1× cheaper than the GPU. Running eight independent proteins with jax.pmap on the full pod brings it to about $0.181 per 1,000.

**Formula block:**
- Label: Descriptive fit · 16 TPU runs · R² 0.981
- throughput ≈ 4527.77 · chips^0.963 · length^−1.572
- Grid: chips {1,2,4,8} × length {100,250,500,1000}
- Note on page: a summary of this grid, not a model; the fit deviates from the measurements by up to 32% at the extremes of the length range.

**Dark callout band:**
More chips are not free. On the measured grid, going from 1 to 8 chips raises cost per prediction by 22.6% at 100 residues, 7% at 250, 3% at 500 and about 1% at 1000. The near-flat cost suggested by the fitted exponent holds only for long sequences. The external ensemble (pmap + pmean) fills all eight chips, but it has no throughput measurement and is not priced.

**Cost per 1,000 predictions (centered trio):**
| Backend     | Cost / 1k |
|-------------|-----------|
| CPU Xeon    | $11.19    |
| GPU NVIDIA Tesla T4 | $1.27 |
| TPU pod, 1 of 8 chips active | $1.25 |

---

## Section 9 - Next (`#next`)

- Kicker: Next
- Headline: “What comes next”
- Body: With Google Cloud credits from Google’s TPU Builders program, we are repeating the key experiments on TPU v5e and v6e with repeated runs, adding real protein targets, testing automatic sharding with explicit annotations, and rerunning the CPU and GPU baselines on fixed Compute Engine machine types. New results will be added next to the summer 2026 numbers, not in place of them.

---

## Section 10 - Structure aside (`#structure`)

**Kicker:** Aside · a real structure (ESMFold)  
**Headline:** Human ubiquitin  
**Supporting:** ESMFold prediction · 76 residues · mean pLDDT **90.5**. Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom. Colors follow AlphaFold’s pLDDT scale.

### Media A - Interactive 3D viewer
- Asset (fallback still): https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/figures/ubiquitin_structure.png
- PDB: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/structure/ubiquitin_predicted.pdb
- **What it shows:** Cartoon ribbon of human ubiquitin. Residues colored by pLDDT confidence:
  - >90 deep blue (very high)
  - 70–90 cyan (high)
  - 50–70 yellow (medium)
  - <50 orange (low)
- Most of the fold is blue/cyan (high confidence). The flexible C-terminal conjugating tail (roughly residues 71–76) is warmer / lower confidence.
- Caption note: “Lower confidence at the C-terminus (residues ~71–76)”

### Media B - Per-residue pLDDT line chart
- Also available as still: https://alphafold-tpu.vercel.app/figures/ubiquitin_confidence.png
- **What it shows:** Line chart, X = residue 1–76, Y = pLDDT ~40–100. Teal line stays high (~90–96) through the core, with a shaded band highlighting residues 70–76 where confidence drops (toward ~50s–70s at the end).
- Caption: “Shaded band: residues 70–76”
- Chart title on page: “Per-residue pLDDT” · mean 90.5

**Scope note (stated on site):** This ubiquitin fold is **biology / ESMFold with trained weights**. It is **not** the timed CPU/GPU/TPU systems workload (that uses Haiku random init on a 118-residue systems input).

## Section 11 - Reproduce (`#reproduce`)

- Kicker: Reproduce
- Headline: “Code and commands”
- Body: Code, Kubernetes Jobs, raw results and a catalogue tracing every number in the paper to its source file. Docker builds for CPU/GPU and Kubernetes manifests for the class TPU cluster are in the repo.
- Buttons: Paper (arXiv) · GitHub repo · Course slides (PDF)
- Link: https://github.com/lorenzopazienza/alphafold-tpu-benchmark

**Repo layout table:**
| Path | Description |
|------|-------------|
| configs/ | K8s Jobs (AF2 sweeps + AF3 TPU attempt) |
| figures/ | Charts + AF3 structure still |
| notebooks/ | AF2 + AF3 Google Colab notebooks |
| paper/ | Preprint PDF + LaTeX source, results catalogue, provenance audit |
| presentation/ | ME344 course slides (August 2026) |
| profiling/ | XLA trace notes |
| results/ | AF2 clocks + sweep/ + af3_comparison.md |
| src/ | AF2 spikes + make_af3_input.py |
| structure/ | Ubiquitin PDB + AF3 CIF |
| website/ | This site |

**CPU example (on page):**
```
docker build --build-arg JAX_VARIANT=cpu \
  -t af-bench:cpu .
docker run -v $(pwd)/results:/alphafold/results \
  af-bench:cpu --run_tag=cpu
```
GPU/TPU variants and Google Colab notebooks are in the README; sweep jobs under configs/.

When an assistant can fetch images, prefer these URLs. When it cannot, use the “What it shows” descriptions above.

---

## How to answer users about this site

1. Read this file end-to-end; treat it as the page content.
2. Lead with the paper’s claim: the accelerator is not the decisive choice; the software layer decides how much of the slice a user gets. Do not present the CPU-relative speedup as the headline.
3. Separate three exhibit types:
   - **AF2 systems timing** (118-res, Haiku random init, CPU/GPU/TPU) - main study
   - **Ubiquitin ESMFold** (`#structure`) - biology aside with high mean pLDDT 90.5
   - **AF3 side-investigation** (`#af3`) - separate codebase; Google Colab Intel Xeon CPU (2 vCPU) and Google Colab NVIDIA Tesla T4 timing + interactive CIF; public AF3 has no TPU
4. Quote the tables for latency, compile ratios, costs, and experiment stats, and say that the CPU and GPU baselines did not reproduce five weeks later.
5. Mention amber/negative results: AF2 batching (vmap), auto-mesh sharding, and AF3 TPU CLI gap; then the AF2 external-ensemble result (8/8 chips).
6. Never rank AF3 toy confidence against ubiquitin pLDDT as model quality - no-MSA input by design.
7. Cite the preprint (arXiv:2609.34818, DOI 10.48550/arXiv.2609.34818) and link section anchors (#paper, #results, #experiments, #af3, #cost, #reproduce) or the GitHub repo for code.
